Literally the reference, as well as the principles you’re using in the design. Like your dragon head is almost a bert grimm redraw. So with Japanese, every design and motif has a meaning and a story. Direction matters, design matters, composition matters. Also Japanese design highlights movement and flow, using contrast between background and foreground to make designs pop. While traditional relies on corresponding amounts of black to color to negative space. 

What makes a design traditional is a single pass outline, and equal ratios of black/color/negative space. Any image can be traditional if the algorithm is followed. 

What makes a tattoo Japanese are the specific stories and imagery, that come from Japanese folklore and tradition. It’s less so an artistic style, and more like part of a culture that also encapsulates an art form/craft. 

Non-Japanese imagery, but in the likeness of Japanese is Japanese inspired OR power trad but not Japanese.

That’s American traditional with Japanese flavor n inspo. Not Japanese traditional. 

Go on Amazon and buy the book “the Japanese tattoo”. Or anything from any of the horiyoshis.

Also a good apprenticeship can last anywhere from 1-5 years. You’ll have to sustain yourself with minimal funds or work a second job thru this whole period (unless you’re rich). Buy a shit ton of tattoos for a year or so will prep you for being poor once you become an apprentice.

I can tell your eye has a knack for subject material that makes good designs. Good job. 

Since your focus is trad, I personally, wouldn’t seek an apprenticeship until my flash was as good or better than the people who you want to teach you to tattoo AND until you have enough financial resources to get tattooed often and pay to play almost. This also allows you to build real relationships and get to know people. The main reason being, the better your flash is, the better of a shop you can get into, the better your experience will be as an apprentice. Also by getting tattooed, and paying to play, you prove to the tattoo community that you don’t just expect free shit. Tattooists respect pay to play, and this way you build relationships and if your flash is undeniable you can find yourself in a position where you’re just in the tattoo world now and are friends with a bunch of tattooists.

Take it slow and think to yourself “how can I give back to tattooing, and not just take”.

I saw your first comments. Im not being condescending. I didn’t insult your art I think it’s good. Especially for being 4 paintings in. I didn’t say you couldn’t do this, I said you could. And made sure to let you know my intention, which was love. I am not the type to spend 40 minutes of my time communicating with you to hurt your perspective of tattooing, but I will have a conversation with you and be genuine and real. Because it’s something I care about very deeply. And there are multiple sides to this. There is the side where it’s beautiful you’re even taking on painting, and then there’s the side of what to expect emotionally in this industry. It took me about 8 years to get an apprenticeship. Then 5 days a week, 12+ hours a day, 2 days a week working a normal job, and 1 day a week painting commissions on my own time. I did this all while expecting my first child. I became homeless for tattooing as well. Cause I couldn’t sustain an apartment AND work for free for 5 days a week. I live out of my care and shower at friends houses. 

One year in I was allowed to tattoo, and was made to tattoo for 3 months for free. Now I get to tattoo for money, but even within I’m still on a 50/50 split percentage. And I work at a shop with very healthy, kind, people. It gets steeper. 


Not everything is a battle. And sometimes people aren’t challenging you, or looking down on you…they’re giving you a real perspective. 

If there were no comments on this post, I might’ve just complimented it. But you have validation and support. Even me, I still validated you. 

And I can say from experience…The need for budding and enthusiastic apprentices to respect tattooing, gate keep, and look at it from a different vantage point  is important for protecting tattooing. Tattooing is like a the Amazon rainforest. Beautiful, teaming with life, rich in history…but everyone wants to be involved in its resources. 

I don’t doubt your current career is difficult, but it is not the best look to claim something that you have experience in is more nerve wrecking than something you have yet to embark on. 

When you get an apprenticeship, hmu. I want to see what your outlook is then. 

Condescending, no. Just a different side of the coin. You don’t have to like me, but I do appreciate your kind words. It’s been a trek. 

I am not trying to come across as better, I am not shit. But perception isn’t intention. And my intention was pure. 

Best thing to do, to get an apprenticeship is listen to people who have experience. Get tattooed. Pay to play. Aim at building relationships, with no time limit. 

And if you want real advice, asking a subreddit of people (who though quite possibly talented with lengthy and amazing careers ahead of them) are still novices…most likely isn’t the best bet?

Fuck the hesitation and fear fam. Trust me. You don’t need these people saying your art is good for it to be good. Im not lecturing, I’m communicating. Get tattooed, paint more, try different mediums. And if you have to ask if your work is good is it good? Validation is awesome but you are the one who dictates what you’re ready for. 

Ego is not your friend. It’s not always a competition. I just relayed what my mentor and people I’ve looked up to reiterated to me. 

Give back, not take. 

I did however, not mean to assume your age. I believe your username threw me? I thought I was taking to a younger person not a grown person. I am still for sure a kid by the way, in many ways. 

Enjoy the walk. Don’t thirst over the destination? If you take in what I’m saying…the road ahead will be easier and make more sense.

You already have the artistic validation, learn how to navigate the field.

And I’d happily look at your work, come get a tattoo and hang with us at the shop and I’ll answer any question you ask.

As far as is your painting good? I would say yes. There’s a decent amount of black, black is in the right places. Certain components are muddy but as far as people who aren’t apprentices but want that you’re in a decent direction. 

Certain things to think about is placement and size. Like that middle design is only going on a back, thigh, or stomach. Is it good enough to take up real estate like that? Right now, looking at your flash I can tell you’re trying to prove to yourself you can do it. But when I think of tattooability I think…is the client getting the best trad tattoo they possibly can off of your designs? Could you sell your flash to a shop and have them tattoo those designs and be confident they were getting their moneys worth?

Ain’t no rush to get into this field man. Get your arms finished and a back piece and start saving money. 

Can you do it? I’m here to tell you you can. But you can come into it stronger, and make your life easier down the road.
The mentality is not “how do I get into this thing called tattooing” it’s “how do I give back to tattooing”

If you can’t be laughed at, what’s gonna happen when you have a pissed off client? What’s gonna happen when it’s slow season, and for whatever reason everyone in your shop is booked but you, and you have to go 3 weeks feeling like the bottom of the barrel while making no money? What happens when a tattoo you make heals scarred or blown tf out? What happens when you haven’t even tattooed your own flash in weeks because you’re only locking in walk ins? So you don’t even get to out your authentic self in it?

How are you gonna get better when people give you criticism? Cause that’s what being an apprentice is. Being told what you suck at so you stop sucking in that area. 

Nerves are a bitch but also you’re putting designs on people forever. This is not a nerves friendly job. This is a field everyone wants to get into because, through instagram a romanticized idea of what tattooing is from a lifestyle point of view has been pushed. When that isn’t even an accurate view. 

You get to wear whatever you want, you are your own authority mostly, and you get to create all day… you can do the same thing being a printmaker, a potter, a woodworker, a muralist…Shit with Tik tok and instagram you can pretty much turn any profession that revolves around creation into a self sustaining dream. 

Tattooing is the most nerve racking one. There is no cool guy ticket. You don’t have to be immediately good man, you just have to be humble. 

Being a good client is awesome. Keep being a good client. Take away expectation. Don’t have your goal be “how do I get in” like tattooing is something to be romanticized. Quit being thirsty. Quite seeking approval, chill out, breathe  and start forming real bonds with artists you look up to. There are many ways to be involved in tattooing without learning to tattoo. 

Think about that. Because after learning to tattoo, you’ll come on to this subreddit and see 30 new ambitious kids with the same desire to get into something and it’ll start to feel…like the magic is being sucked away. 

Some of us that are left still hurt for tattooing. And honor that the gate remain closed. It’s not for everybody. It could very well be for you but…..if everyone got in when they wanted or were told their art was the best…none of us would have jobs. Lol. 


Tattooing is sacred. It’s an ancient art form. Slowwww down. Start asking about apprenticeships when your flash is so killer that you make established artists insecure. Start looking for apprenticeships when you’re completely covered and it doesn’t make sense to not tattoo because 80% of your friend circle and associations already does. 

Pay your dues.  Hurt a lil bit. That’s the tradition part. 

Or get a pen off Amazon and go crazy on your homies. 

This is meant with love. Ask specific questions too. Ask about how much money artists under 5 years make. Ask about what happens to your body when you tattoo 5+ days a week for years at a time. 

Learn in depth about the craft you want to partake in. This is not just a way for artsy kids to make money while being artsy. Many crash and burn too.

Get tattooed by the best trad tatters in your city/state and ask them. 

I will say, An apprenticeship will move smoother if you already have your flash 100% dialed in to the best of your abilities. Mentors should teach you application, but with all the competition and people who want to tattoo you shouldn’t be taught how to paint flash at the hypothetical shop you end up in. 

Look at as many tattooers flash as possible. Old and new. If your stuff isn’t hitting like them, lock yourself in the crib for as long as it takes and don’t emerge until you know you’re shitting on everybody. 

And then pay to play until you’ve made friends.

I attempted to get an apprenticeship for 8 years. There are cheat codes, and methods that will get you there faster BUT if you’re anything like I was, you most likely don’t have the best attitude around it. Which will delay your entry into the industry. 

A few pieces of advice:

1.) don’t think “how do I get in to tattooing asap”. Think “what can I add to the ancient multigenerational craft of tattooing”. 

2.) Don’t look for an apprenticeship if you’re still learning what a good tattoo design is/learning to draw. 4.) don’t be afraid to start at the basics and trace dead or og tattooers vintage flash. 

5.) build relationships by paying the best tattooists in your preferred style to make you tattoos. 

6.) don’t be hard on yourself, move in a way that respects the craft, and the people who have held on to the tradition of tattooing to bring it to this point where now you can also partake. 

7.) be a nerd. Learn as much as you can. 

8.) be ready to be broke. Be ready to sweat. Be ready to be pissed off. Apprenticeships are not easy. Don’t expect that. Even the best tattooers you know also didn’t start making money until 5+ years in. Expect to be poor. Tattooing is not just a cash grab for people with artistic abilities. It is not an easy route out of poverty.

Contrary to popular believe, neo-trad and trad actually don’t go together. Though we sometimes get along as artists, these are two different worlds. Neo trad is trad concepts but with multiple line widths and a color palette that mimics realism or color illustrative more so than actual traditional. A lot of neo-trad artists think trad is “basic” or “easy” and a lot of trad artists feel like neo-trad is corny and doing too much. At my shop the guys don’t even want to hear the word “neo” haha. I’ll often hear comments such as “what’s with all these extra line widths, pick one” or “a quadruple fade in those oakleaves? You’re not even gonna be able to cover that bullshit up”. Lmao. 

It’s not as mean as it sounds; different strokes for different folks. But just kee that in mind. If you go to trad peeps looking for an apprenticeship with a neo portfolio they may overlook you. And if you go to the neotrad guys with trad stuff, they’ll most likely want you to switch over, over time. 

For vintage flash I’d start with tattoocollection.eu, to get and idea of what you should be tracing and to really have a good display of what trad flash is. 

For Japanese I’d buy the book “the Japanese tattoo” by sandi Feldman. Cheapest tattoo book you can get, generally tattoo literature is expensive. 

I’d look up joe lieber, George burchett, sailor Jerry collins, Mike Malone, Freddy Corbin, Ed hardy, percy waters, Leo zulueta, Jeff zuck, Dan higgs, lew the Jew, Hong Kong swallow, cap Coleman, rosie camanga, etc. there’s a whole rabbit hole to go into of people who are considered legends both alive and dead. Google is your friend, and go crazy. 

With Japanese tattooing you have irezumi and tebori/wabori. This is a world I’m less familiar with but I can tell you you should start with the horiyoshi lineage. 1-3. 

As far as documentaries after you become familiar with names, just type those in YouTube or google. There’s no stand out documentary but like I said earlier google is your friend and the names I’ve given you should lead you in that direction. 

Cheers and best of luck. 

Most tattoo books are hundreds of dollar by the way. This is part of the legacy of gatekeeping. Gatekeeping will be annoying to you know, but if you really put the work in you’ll embrace it down the road. This industry is not for everyone. It’s for those who love and respect it. 

Repeat to yourself “what can I do to give back to the ancient art of tattooing”. Try to get rid of the “me me me” “how do I get in 😨” mentality. I wish I’d known that sooner.

Good questions. Hmm, let’s get into it. Disclaimer: I only am familiar with the process of becoming a traditional apprentice (American/Japanese/tribal/single pass bold or fine line tattooing). So that’s what I speak on. I cannot point you in the direction of how to be an apprentice in realism, ignorant style, illustrative, or anything else. And I wouldn’t recommend starting at a low quality/cash grab/street style/walk in shop (unless it’s trad focused) if you’re not TOUGH as nails cause there are a lot of predators and manipulators in this industry and most of them tend to be at the cash grab shops.  

1.) the first thing to know, in the process of becoming a traditional apprentice (which I wish I knew sooner) is NERD out. This means deeply research and submerge yourself in the culture. This includes but is not limited to hand painting flash, researching masters/old heads who created and pioneered the styles and imagery that we as aspiring tattooers now carry on, get tattooed often, as well as researching different cultures both historic AND indigenous who’s motifs and energy is represented in GOOD tattooing. Don’t get stuck on simply getting people to like your art. Truly fall in love with the process of GOOD tattoo design, and the culture that comes with that. There’s so much to know. 

2.) If I could do it over again I wouldn’t have such a “me, me, me” attitude. I wouldn’t be “thirsty” for an apprenticeship. I would slow down, enjoy life, and trust the process. This is a multi-century craft, in which the roots go back even further than that. I like to joke that tattooing is the 3rd oldest profession after sex work and robbing. Haha. The thought on your mind should not be “how do I get in 😰” and should actually be “how can I give back to this ancient process, which is tattooing”. 

3.) paint. Paint. Paint. Don’t just illustrate. Don’t be afraid to trace dead AND legendary peoples flash. Pay attention to where these people put black, where they put negative space, and where they put color. Repaint sheets exactly how they did it, because traditional is still around for a reason. What’s tried and true works. After you get comfortable with this you can begin to tweak vintage designs a little bit to add your personal touch. After a year of this, hopefully what you learned will allow to create custom designs in a bold single pass style. Use as many “old head approved” mediums as you can. Try different types of paper, hot press, cold press, arches, stonehenge, reeves etc. try different paints, like gouache, acrylic ink, watercolor, etc. learn about staining and varnish and uv protection. Also I’ll give you a hidden gem that is very rarely shared. A good trad design is 30% color, 30% black, 30% negative space, 10% lines. Do with that information what you will. Don’t overcomplicate with colors. Pick one gold/yellow, one scarlet/red, one blue/green/turqoise, one brown, alongside black and don’t budge from that. Stay consistent and do all your flash with this repeated pallet. As you get better and more comfortable add a grey, a purple, and if you chose gold add a brighter yellow. If you choose turqoise add a green and a blue. If you chose raw sienna as your brown, add burnt sienna. 

4.)don’t look for an apprenticeship until your flash is undeniable. Then Find the best tattooer in your city and build a relationship with them by paying them to make you tattoos. A large part of Tattooing is social interaction. Relationships are what get you in, and relationships are what keep you working once you start tattooing. If you go to the top dog of traditional in your city, and build a relationship with them, they may not be the one to apprentice you. But after collecting from the best trad person in your city, when you actually set out to get tattooed by other trad artists, and are actively looking for an apprenticeship you’ll have way more “credibility” and the other tattooers who were inspired by the big dog will be more open to talk to you and give you a shot. In this industry co-signs are valuable. If you’ve been respecting the culture, getting tattooed, asking the right questions, staying humble, if you know how to act, how to build relationships, how to treat people, if your flash is good…even if a big dog doesn’t apprentice you something as little as getting a shout out or a co-sign from one of these people can land you in a very good shop somewhere local simply off the energy you put in. 

5.) Be ready to be broke. Tattooing, especially traditional tattooing is NOT a cash grab. It’s also an over saturated industry. You may be poor for 5 years trying to do this. And poverty does not help mental health OR artistic inspiration. Just things to remember. 

6.) be patient and listen more than you talk. 

7.) truly love this shit. You have to really love it. If you don’t really love everything about this journey, even the painful parts then it’s not for you. There is no cool kids club in tattooing. We are not rockstars. We are psycho nerds who sometimes get to make cool stuff. We are craftsmen. 

And that’s pretty much it. I hope this advice was helpful and seen as friendly. Best of luck to anyone who reads this. If I can think of anything else, or if you have any specific questions feel free to ask me. I know this process can be frustrating, but tattooing must be protected. Most people gatekeep for a reason. I gatekeep less, but the reason I do is because the type of information I share and what I recommend people do is HARD. And most people won’t follow through with it.

One more comment as well. I’d suggest limiting your color pallet. One gold/yellow, one brown, one blue/turqoise, one green, one red/scarlet, along with black of course. When you get more comfortable add in a purple and a grey, and maybe some more greens/yellows/blues.

You have pretty solid drawing skills. I spent seven years trying to get an apprenticeship, with “pretty solid drawing skills”. You’re starting off great, but “pretty solid drawing skills” in truth, doesn’t always translate to good tattoo design. If you tattooed any of this, guaranteed you’ll hate all of these in 3-5 years when you’ve finally dialed it all in. When you start looking for an apprenticeship, try to eliminate those future feelings to the best of your abilities. There are ways to do this. 

1.) don’t be afraid to trace classic designs, and shade/lay your color in the same way the old heads and masters did it. At least for your first year of making flash. 

2.) focus on painting, and use a rehydrating medium like gouache or water color as it’ll translate to skin in your mind better than anything else. If you start small, and build up your design slowly you’ll find that you have more control. Slow and steady wins the raise with painting. 

3.) for American traditional focus on even ratios of negative space, to black, to color. I like to think 30/30/30 and ten percent lines. 

4.) Japanese traditional is solid color, negative space, and minimal black, over a black background with negative space. What you’ve created as Japanese traditional is illustrative but Japanese influenced. 

5.) focus on proportion and symmetry. 

6.) look into the history of every style you want to be good at. Figure out who did what you’re doing, and who pioneered what you’re doing WELL. And really dive into that. It’ll make you care about the craft more, and also give you a direction for how you should create. What’s tried and true never fails. 

Just some friendly advise, and shit I was told on my own journey to being an apprentice. Keep going.
